I swear I see it all the time in politics. Like someone will say that a woman has a right to choose what she does with her body, but another will say a baby has the right to life. Both of those are true. So why does the argument then become about who's rights to take away rather than how to reconcile these truths? Once we've defined what's true shouldn't we try to decide how best to solve a difficult situation to make it as fair as possible for all parties?

That may be a bad example, but what do you think?
Have you ever felt like both sides of a polarized issue present valid observations, but present them as if they are conflicting?
Idk but did you see the post about the Hegelian principle the other day?

Hegelian speaking the struggle between a thesis and an antithesis produces a new thesis so our beliefs , laws , norms, morals and in general all manifestations of rules commanding our social activities are results of conflict . Usually those conflicts are between valid arguments that one of them got invalidated or just wore off by change because what seems logical now may not be tomorrow .

Coming to your example if mankind was facing extinction nobody would care about women's reproductive rights and if earth was overpopulated babies would be aborted years after their birth but since neither of those variables are true the abortion debate presents two valid and conflicting arguments , at least for now .

Especially in politics, neither side is interested in reconciling truths, but rather in convincing you, the observer, to side with them.

If they talked intelligently about the different perspectives of the issue, and did not portray them as mutually exclusive to each other, then the time that each side spent on that discussion would have been time "wasted" since it was not spent winning more supporters.

In politics, that's what it's all about: The "sides" have already made up their minds about what is right, and want to convince you to join them in their conviction.

If you are looking for a discussion that will lead you or observers towards greater understanding, rather than "picking a side," politics is the wrong venue. Perhaps a book club or a philosophy course at a good university with a good professor. I honestly have no idea if there's any public institution where you could go for that kind of discussion of issues.

The "woman's right to choose" is a strawman that was invented by activist pro-choicers so they wouldn't have to deal with arguing over whether a baby is a human being. It's honestly a coward's way out. However, since it's become the mantra, many newer pro-choice advocates embrace it without thinking it through.

I am pro-choice because I believe that a "person" is the sum of their thoughts, dreams, aspirations, and memories. The lump of meat is just a lump of meat. So a fetus isn't really a person. I personally don't have an issue with the death of a fetus up until birth, but I recognize that puts me at odds with most of humanity. So I draw the line as "can live outside the uterus" and yes - that also contradicts superhuman neonatal care.

We can split hairs on that, but there is my argument. I suspect that a whole bunch of people, if we got the screaming prolife zealots out of their face, would agree with the general concept at least during the first two trimesters.

Pro-lifers argue that a fetus is a "human" from conception. Personally I think they're insane, and disagree with them on the basis that two cells is not a fucking human by any stretch of the imagination.

So... all that being said...

The "woman's right to choose" bullshit is essentially saying that if I own a hotel, I can shoot a guest if I don't want them in my building. It's my hotel, and I have the right to decide what happens inside it. Saying I can't randomly kill guests is intruding on my right to choose.

I've tried this on a few pro-choicers and boy do they get angry. It's really fun - I highly recommend it.

As a side note - a LOT of people who get worked up about issues honestly cannot understand the concept that you're on the same side as them and just trying to tell them they're arguing wrong.
